summary: Describes an architecture for securing Internet routing, built on the Resource Public Key Infrastructure. The RPKI reflects how IP address space and AS numbers are allocated, and a distributed repository stores the signed objects. A first use is letting the holder of address space authorize which network may originate routes for it. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: On the Internet, routers learn paths from each other by trusting what they are told, so a network can claim to hold addresses that belong to someone else. This memo describes a supporting infrastructure that fixes that: a system of certificates, mirroring the way addresses are handed down from the global registry to regions and then to network operators, that proves who holds which addresses and AS numbers, plus signed statements saying which networks are allowed to announce which addresses. Routers can then check those statements before trusting an announcement.

questions: how to secure bgp route origin
what is a route origination authorization
how does rpki secure bgp origin
subtitle: An architecture that lets the holder of an IP address block or a set of AS numbers prove that ownership, so routers can check who may originate a route.

tldr.problem: BGP carries no proof that the network announcing a route is entitled to the addresses in it, so anyone can announce someone else's prefix and attract traffic.
tldr.mechanism: A public key infrastructure tied to the existing address allocation hierarchy issues certificates that attest to holdings of IP addresses and AS numbers, and signed objects called route origin authorizations state which ASes may originate which prefixes.
tldr.outcome: It is the architectural foundation of the Resource Public Key Infrastructure, published in February 2012 and widely deployed as part of securing inter-domain routing.

today: RFC 6480 is an Informational RFC published in February 2012, and the unit metadata records no successor. It is the architectural document that the Resource Public Key Infrastructure is built on, with companion RFCs defining the certificate profile, the signed objects and the validation rules that this memo points to.

sections.title: An Infrastructure for Routing Security
sections.content:
This document describes an architecture for an infrastructure to support improved security for BGP routing. It has three principal elements: a Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI), digitally signed routing objects to support routing security, and a distributed repository system to hold the PKI objects and the signed routing objects.

The architecture lets an entity verifiably assert that it is the legitimate holder of a set of IP addresses or a set of Autonomous System numbers. Its first application shows how a legitimate holder of address space can explicitly and verifiably authorize one or more ASes to originate routes to that space, and such authorizations could be used to build BGP route filters more securely. The design also aims to support future security protocols for routing. It applies to the routing of both IPv4 and IPv6 datagrams, and use with address families such as MPLS labels is out of scope.

To ease deployment, the architecture reuses existing standards wherever possible. It builds on the X.509 certificate profile and on the certificate extensions for representing IP addresses and AS numbers, and it uses the Cryptographic Message Syntax as the syntax for the signed objects it defines. Because the structure of the PKI follows the existing resource allocation structure, managing it is a natural extension of the work the registries already do.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal has three parts: a system of certificates, a set of signed statements about routes, and a way to publish and fetch them. It leans on existing, well-understood standards so the people who already manage addresses can take on the new work without inventing much.

sections.title: Certificates That Attest to Resources
sections.content:
Because the holder of a block of address space is entitled to define where traffic to that block should go, inter-domain routing decisions rest on knowledge of how address space is allocated. The architecture therefore provides cryptographically verifiable attestations of those allocations. The allocation is hierarchical: the root is IANA, below it are the Regional Internet Registries, and below them come national registries, local registries and ISPs, and subscribers with provider-independent allocations. A certificate attests to an allocation, and issuing a subordinate certificate corresponds to sub-allocating resources, so the same PKI can express both IP address and AS number allocations.

Certificates in this PKI are called resource certificates. They bind the public key in the certificate to the IP addresses or AS numbers listed in the certificate's delegation extensions. An important property distinguishes this PKI from most others: certificates do not attest to the identity of the subject. The subject names are deliberately not descriptive, because the design intends to provide authorization rather than authentication. That spares issuers the cost and liability of verifying that an entity is entitled to use a subject name, which makes it easier for them to act as certification authorities. A common name must still be unique among the subjects a given authority certifies.

The PKI contains two broad kinds of certificate. CA certificates attest to address and AS number holdings and are needed by anyone who sub-allocates resources; a CA certificate is also needed to issue a route origin authorization, because an end-entity certificate must be issued to validate each one. End-entity certificates, issued by resource holder CAs, are used to validate route origin authorizations and other signed objects such as manifests.
sections.plainLanguage: The certificates here are unusual: they say which addresses and AS numbers a holder has, but not who the holder is. That is on purpose, because the goal is to prove what resources you control, not your name. Some certificates belong to organizations that hand addresses down to others; others are used to sign individual statements about routes.

sections.title: The Hierarchy and the Repositories
sections.content:
The PKI mirrors the way resources are handed out. Each certificate is issued by the level above, and a holder may sub-allocate parts of its block to itself or to another organization subject to the registries' contracts, so the chain of certificates follows the chain of allocation. AS numbers follow the same pattern with one difference: by convention they may not be sub-allocated except by a regional or national registry, and yet both kinds of resource can be expressed in the same PKI.

Each level in this hierarchy is a potential certification authority, and each needs a way to publish what it has signed. The architecture therefore includes a distributed repository system, which holds both the PKI objects and the signed routing objects and makes them available to the ISPs that use them in routing decisions. A relying party fetches a resource holder's certificates and signed objects from these repositories, validates them against a trust anchor, and so obtains a verified statement about who holds what and who is authorized to originate which routes.

The structure means that the entities already responsible for allocating addresses and AS numbers become the operators of the certification authorities at their level, and existing allocation and revocation practices have direct counterparts in the design.
sections.plainLanguage: The system copies the address hand-out tree: the global registry certifies the regional ones, which certify the networks below them, and so on. Each of those levels publishes what it signs in a repository that anyone can fetch from, and a router or other user checks the signed material back up the chain to a trusted starting point.

sections.title: Signed Objects: Manifests and Authorizations
sections.content:
Beyond certificates, the infrastructure relies on non-certificate signed objects, including route origin authorizations and manifests. A route origin authorization is a signed object in which an address holder gives an explicit authorization that a given AS is permitted to originate routes to a set of addresses. This is the first and central application of the architecture, and it provides the cryptographic validation that an AS is authorized to originate routes to a prefix. A relying party that has validated a route origin authorization can use it, for example, to construct route filters.

Manifests exist to protect the repository system itself. Because signed objects live in a distributed repository rather than a single trusted server, an attacker who gains access to a repository could withhold or replace objects. A manifest lists the objects that should be present and is itself signed, so a relying party can detect objects that have been removed or substituted. The design mentions separately that revocation has a counterpart in this architecture, matching the existing practice of withdrawing resources.

All of this signed material is expressed in the Cryptographic Message Syntax, which keeps the new objects within well-understood existing syntax rather than inventing a fresh one.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kinds of signed statement do most of the work. A route origin authorization says which network is allowed to announce which addresses, and a manifest lists what should be published so missing or swapped files can be spotted. Both are written in an existing, well-tested format.

sections.title: What It Does and Does Not Prove
sections.content:
The architecture provides authorization, not authentication, and it is important to be clear about the difference. A validated resource certificate proves that the issuer granted the holder the listed addresses or AS numbers; it does not prove anything about who the holder is. Because the certificates do not carry identity, a validated route origin authorization tells a relying party that whoever holds the relevant resources authorized a given AS to originate their prefixes, which is exactly the fact needed to filter routes, and no more.

The design also assumes its inputs are trustworthy in ways it does not itself secure. It depends on the registries to allocate and revoke resources correctly, and on the correctness of the underlying certificate profile, the resource extensions, and the signed-object syntax. It does not by itself validate the routes that BGP carries or the path attributes attached to them; it validates origination authorization. The distributed repository is a point that needs protection, which is why manifests are part of the architecture.

The document is an architecture, not a complete protocol suite. It sets out the components and how they fit together and points to the companion specifications that define the certificate profile, the signed objects and their validation.
sections.plainLanguage: What the system proves is limited and precise: that the recognized holder of a block of addresses allowed a particular network to announce them. It does not prove who anyone is, and it does not check the paths that route announcements travel. Those limits are deliberate, and they keep the design focused on the question routers need answered.
